4.4 — Attack: Close-Range Contact Damage

The enemy can find you, and now it can reach you. "Touch equals minus one health" sounds like the easiest line in the unit. It is not, because the callback that detects the touch runs sixty times a second — and so does the player's death rule from 2.2. Today you make contact hurt at a rate a human can survive, and you choose which of three hazard models does the work.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I stop a contact hit hurting me sixty times a second?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

When the enemy reaches me it should cost me health — and it should not cost me the whole bar in a third of a second. "Touching hurts" is the whole feature, and there is nothing in it yet that a computer can act on.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Decide when a hit is allowed to landwhat does this part do?Read: the hazard-model table above, and the OnCollisionEnter2D, OnCollisionStay2D and OnTriggerStay2D rows of this lesson's reference table
  2. Confirm the thing you touched is the playerwhat does this part do?Read: the CompareTag row of this lesson's reference table, and the coin check you wrote in 2.1
  3. Rate-limit the hitwhat does this part do?Read: the Time.time and cooldown rows of this lesson's reference table, and your own firing gate from 3.3
  4. Deliver the damage through the method you already wrotewhat does this part do?Read: the GetComponent and method-call rows of this lesson's reference table, and the health method you wrote in 2.2
  5. Decide what does not happen to the enemywhat does this part do?Read: your own projectile callback from 3.4, and the Destroy row that lesson priced

Four of these five parts are lessons you have already finished. A tag check is 2.1, the method and its sign are 2.2, the gate is 3.3, and the reach across to another script is 3.4. The genuinely new one is the first: until today every hazard you built stood still, and a hazard that moves changes which callback is correct. That decision is what everything below it hangs on.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make contact hurt" cannot be looked up. "Compare the clock against the moment of the last hit" can — and you wrote that comparison in 3.3.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The reading prices three models for when a hit lands and three ways to reach the player's health. Name the two you chose, and say what each one costs you — in your own words, not the table's.

The enemy's animator from 4.2 has an Attack trigger waiting for it. Which of your own fields has to be true before that trigger fires so the picture and the damage agree — and what does the player see when the animation plays and no damage lands?

In 2.2 you wrote one method that changes health by a signed amount, plus a rule that fires when health reaches zero. Read your own arithmetic before you answer: which sign is the one that hurts — and does the death rule test a separate flag, or the number itself?

3.3 fixed a turret that fired sixty times a second with two fields and one condition. Which of the three models in the table above rebuilds that exact bug on an enemy, and what do those two fields become inside a collision callback?

3.4's bullet reached into the player's health and then destroyed itself. Which part of today's split is that same reach — and which part is where the enemy deliberately does not do what the bullet did?

1.3 taught you where a value has to be declared before it can survive from one frame to the next. Which part above depends on that rule, and what does the remembered moment hold if you declare it in the wrong place?

The Problem: Touching You Is Too Cheap ~20 min

Your goal: standing against the enemy should cost health, at a rate the player can react to. You have already built one hazard in this project and chosen how it would hurt you. Read those three options again — they are the same three, but the object wearing them has changed: this one moves. And a moving hazard can be solid or a trigger, so the third model below appears twice, once for each collider you could have given the enemy in 4.1. Three models, four rows — and the price column is the one that decides it:

Hazard modelWhat firesWhat the player feelsWhat it costs you
A solid enemy, touched once OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) You bump into it and lose health once per bump. Damage lands on the frame the two shapes meet and never again while they stay in contact — one hit per pass, not one per frame you lean on it, which is how the coin counted a pickup in 2.1. The cost is the exploit: an enemy can pin you against a wall and you take nothing further, so the safest place in the fight becomes the inside of the enemy. A solid enemy also shoves your Dynamic player around, which is either the fight you designed in 4.1 or a fight you did not.
A trigger enemy, passed through once OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) It walks through you and one hit lands as it passes. A trigger is a sensor, not a wall: it reports what already happened and never shoves anybody — the same distinction as the coin versus the spike in 2.2. Buying that costs you the enemy's solidity: it passes through your walls unless you handle that separately, and a chaser that catches you and stops on top of you deals damage exactly once and then nothing at all, which is the wrong answer for a hunter.
A drain while contact lasts, with a cooldown
solid flavour		 OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D collision) It holds you against itself and your health drains at a steady, readable rate for as long as you stay there. The Stay callbacks fire on every physics step — sixty times a second. With no rate limit your entire health bar is gone in about a third of a second, because 2.2's death rule is only a comparison against zero. This is the one model that needs the cooldown from 3.3, and building that cooldown is the whole of today. It also keeps the shove: a solid enemy physically decides where the fight happens, and a player pinned in a corner is now being punished for it instead of spared.
A drain while contact lasts, with a cooldown
trigger flavour		 OnTriggerStay2D(Collider2D other) It overlaps you and your health drains at the same steady rate for as long as it stays inside you. Identical every-frame cost and the identical fix: the cooldown. What the trigger buys you is a fight that stays wherever the player stands — nothing is shoved, and the enemy passes through walls — which is either the hunter you designed in 4.1 or a haunting. Is Trigger has to be ticked to match this callback name, or the Console stays empty.
The parameter types differ, and it changes what you can write. OnTrigger* hands you a Collider2D, which has .gameObject and .CompareTag directly. OnCollision* hands you a Collision2D — a data container with contact points and relativeVelocity — so the tag check becomes collision.gameObject.CompareTag(...). One extra hop, and one extra chance to write it wrong. The checkbox and the callback name have to agree: Is Trigger ticked gives you the OnTrigger* callback, unticked gives you the OnCollision* one, and an unticked collider with a trigger callback in your file is not an error — it is silence.

Whichever model you choose, the enemy still has to reach the player's health. That is a second decision, and there is more than one honest answer:

How the enemy reaches the player's healthWhat it looks likeWhat it costs you
From the thing it touched Ask the collided object for the PlayerController component. No wiring at all, and it works on every copy of the prefab. The lookup only happens on the frames a contact occurs, which is exactly when you can afford it.
Up the hierarchy from the thing it touched Ask the collided object's parents for the PlayerController. Survives a collider that lives on a child object — which is your situation if you put the player's collider on Sprite in 2.1. Costs a slightly longer search, and it can find a component you did not expect further up.
A [SerializeField] reference on each enemy Drag the Player into a slot in the Inspector. Zero lookup cost and visible on the Inspector. But there are four enemies in the Overworld and each needs wiring — and it breaks the day the player is created at runtime instead of placed in the scene.
The every-frame problem, one more time. In 3.3 the turret fired once per frame because a condition was true for sixty frames in a row. The Stay callbacks are the same disease. This is not a coincidence and it is not a Unity quirk — it is what "run this while the condition holds" means in every engine. The cure is the same too: a cooldown gate. Read the next table for the API, then build it.

Socratic: Choosing a Hazard Model

  1. Which of the four rows in the table did you choose, and what does the player learn to do about it after two encounters?
  2. If you chose OnCollisionEnter2D alone, what happens when a chasing enemy pins you against a wall? Is that a fair fight, or an exploit?
  3. You built a hazard once already, in 2.2. What is the difference between that hazard and this one — and does a moving hazard change which model is correct?
  4. At 60 frames per second with a damage value of one and no cooldown, what is the player's health after half a second of contact? Work it out against the health maximum you set in 2.3, then test it.
  5. What should the cooldown field be seeded with so the very first contact hurts immediately? If you seed it to 0, how long is the free grace period you just invented — and is that a feature or an accident?
  6. A bullet was destroyed when it hurt you in 3.4. Is the enemy destroyed when it hurts you? Explain the difference in terms of what kind of object each one is.
Read the Docs: The API for a Contact Hit ~15 min

This is the level-3 substitute for a walkthrough. The API is laid out below and the code is not: you write the file. Between them, these rows are the whole job — a callback, a tag check, a lookup, a call, a rate limit and three declarations. Every one of them costs something, so name the cost before you pick; otherwise you are not choosing, you are guessing.

SignatureWhat you getWhat it costs you
OnCollisionEnter2D
void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) — a callback. Unity calls it; you never do.		 Fires on the first frame two solid colliders meet, with a body on at least one of the pair — the rule from 2.1, and the player has carried a Dynamic body since 2.2. The parameter is the other object's collision. Once per entry, and only once: the shapes have to separate and meet again for a second message, so an enemy that pins you deals nothing further. Misspelling the name is not an error, it is silence.
OnTriggerEnter2D
void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) — a callback		 Fires on the first frame two shapes overlap, with Is Trigger ticked on at least one of them. The parameter is the other object's collider. One message per pass, not one per frame of leaning — a sensor that reports and never shoves. It also means the enemy is not a wall any more, which is a decision you made about its collider in 4.1.
OnCollisionStay2D
void OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D collision) — a callback		 A message on every physics step the two solid colliders remain in contact — sixty of them a second. The message does not mean "a hit happened", it means "the condition is still true". Without the rate limit below, your death rule from 2.2 resolves the encounter in about a third of a second. A Kinematic body reports nothing against a static wall — it only collides with Dynamic bodies, which is what your player is.
OnTriggerStay2D
void OnTriggerStay2D(Collider2D other) — a callback		 The same every-physics-step message for two shapes that stay overlapped, with Is Trigger ticked. Identical every-frame cost, and the same cooldown is the answer. One extra thing to trip over: the tag check inside it runs sixty times a second too, so put the cheap check first and the expensive work last.
CompareTag
bool CompareTag(string tag), asked of the object that carries the collider — other.gameObject.CompareTag(...) or collision.gameObject.CompareTag(...)		 Asks the engine whether that object carries the tag, so one check tells you what kind of thing you touched. Exact spelling, and the tag must already exist in the project. It has to be asked of the object you touched, never of the script the callback lives on. And it tells you nothing about what that object can do — that is the next two rows.
GetComponent<T>() / GetComponentInParent<T>()
T GetComponent<T>(), called on a GameObject or a component		 The component of that type on the object you call it on — here, the PlayerController that owns the health. The InParent form keeps walking up the parent chain to find it. Both are searches, and both hand you null when the type is not there. The plain version does not look at children, so the component has to sit on the object you actually touched; reach for InParent only if your player's collider is on a child. InChildren exists too and is the slowest of the three.
A call on another script's method
TakeDamage(int amount) — the method you wrote in 2.2, called on the reference you just looked up		 Hands the problem to the object that owns the data: the enemy never touches the health number, it only asks. The same method serves the spike, the bullet and any healing you add later, because a signed amount can travel both ways. You declared it private in 2.2, and 3.4 is where it was widened so another script could reach it — if your 3.4 hit was detected on PlayerController instead of on the bullet, that never happened and widening it is part of today's work. Read your own method before you pass a number: it subtracts, so the positive amount is the one that hurts, and a sign that is backwards is not a compiler error — it is a heal.
[SerializeField] private int damage
a field declaration, not a call — class body, never inside a method		 A named value that survives every frame and appears in the Inspector as the designer's knob for how punishing one contact is. The type has to match the parameter of the method you call: TakeDamage(int amount) takes an int, so a float knob cannot be passed without a conversion the compiler refuses. And because 2.2's method also holds the death rule, your default is a ratio against the player's maximum health from 2.3 — not a number you happen to like.
The cooldown pair
two fields in the class body: one serialized interval, one private remembered moment		 The rate limit from 3.3, pointed at a callback instead of at Update(): the interval is how often this enemy may hurt the player, the remembered moment is when it last did. Both fields belong in the class body — declared inside the callback, the remembered moment is rebuilt on every call and remembers nothing, which is the same scope rule as 1.3 and looks exactly like a working rate limit until you count the hits. Seed the moment one interval before the scene starts, the way 3.3 seeded its turret, so the first contact hurts immediately instead of serving a penalty for a hit that never happened. And one interval means the second hit inside the window is discarded, not queued: nothing is owed to the player when the window closes.
Time.time
float Time.time		 The seconds since the scene loaded, counting up — the clock your gate is compared against. A moment means nothing on its own; it is only meaningful against another moment on the same clock. If your remembered value is a countdown decremented by Time.deltaTime, that is a different row of 3.3's table and it cannot be compared against this clock.
Debug.Log(object)
void Debug.Log(object message)		 Prints to the Console — the only feedback this game has until Unit 5. Text only, and it prints when you call it. Print the moment damage lands and you can count hits per second against your cooldown knob, which is the only way to prove a rate limit works with no UI at all.
Four facts a signature cannot carry. First, the callback is silent about your mistakes: forget the collider, mistype the method name, or tick the wrong checkbox, and the Console stays empty — "no error at all" is the hardest bug in this unit to find, which is why you check the component before you check the code. Second, the tag check is the first filter and the component lookup is the second, and a lookup that finds nothing hands you null rather than stopping the script, so every line below it has to be written as though the lookup succeeded. Third, the player's health lives on PlayerController and nowhere else — that is where you put it in 2.2. Fourth, the callback knows nothing about your state machine: it fires on any contact between the two colliders, including the frame a calmly patrolling guard walks into you. If damage should only land while the enemy is chasing, that condition is yours to write, and 4.2's Attack trigger is waiting on the same decision.
Build Lab: Make Contact Hurt ~25 min

The enemy's collider and body came from 4.1. The player has had both since 2.1. Everything today is code in EnemyController.cs.

Architectural specification: the model and the knob.

Choosing the model:

  • Which of the three models in the first table did you choose, and which callback name does it give you? Write the name and the parameter type down before you open the file.
  • Is Is Trigger ticked on the enemy's collider — the setting you chose in 4.1 — and does it agree with the callback name you just wrote? The Console will not tell you when they disagree.
  • What does your choice cost the player: a drain they can read, an exploit they can lean on, or an enemy they can now walk through?

The damage knob:

  • What serialized field lets a designer decide how much one hit costs? What type must it match to work with your player's existing health rule?
  • What default do you ship, given the player's maximum health from 2.3 and the number of enemies in the scene? Justify the ratio, not the number.
Architectural specification: the cooldown.
  • Which field records how often this enemy may hurt the player, and which field records when it last did? Name both so the pair reads clearly in the Inspector.
  • Where do those two fields live — in the class body, or inside the callback that uses them? Say what the remembered moment holds on the next call if you declare it inside the method, and why the rate limit looks like it works anyway.
  • What value must the "last hurt" field start at so that the first touch lands instantly? Explain what that seed means in plain English to a partner.
  • Where does the cooldown test sit relative to the tag check — inside it, or before it? Which arrangement avoids doing work for contacts you do not care about?
  • Is the cooldown field public, private, or serialized? Should a designer be able to tune how often the enemy hurts the player without recompiling?
  • Nothing is queued while the gate is shut. If the player runs into two enemies at once, does your interval decide the rate per enemy or per player — and is that the encounter you meant?
Architectural specification: the callback.
  • Which callback method (or methods) did you choose from the table? Write the exact name and the exact parameter type before you type it.
  • How do you confirm the thing you touched is the player? Which of the two parameter types lets you write CompareTag directly, and what must you write for the other?
  • What would happen if you skipped that check entirely and the enemy brushed a wall, a coin or another enemy?
  • The callback fires on any contact, not on "the enemy is attacking". Does your enemy deal damage on its patrol too — and if that is wrong, where does the condition that stops it belong?
Architectural specification: delivering the damage.
  • Which method on PlayerController do you call, and what is its parameter type?
  • How do you get from the collided object to that method — plain GetComponent, GetComponentInParent, or a wired reference? Where is the player's collider, and does your answer match?
  • What guard check protects you if the object carries no PlayerController? What does the error look like without it?
  • Read the line in your own method that changes health, and work out which sign hurts. Name it, then say out loud what the other sign would do to the player instead.
  • Is the method callable from EnemyController.cs yet? If your 3.4 damage was delivered by 3.4's bullet, it is public already; if it was delivered on the player's side, it may still be private and that is part of today.
Architectural specification: what does NOT happen.
  • Is anything destroyed here? Compare this callback to the projectile's in 3.4 and explain the difference in one sentence.
  • Should the enemy stop moving while it attacks, or keep chasing? What does each look like to the player, and what does your animator's Attack trigger do about it? (See 4.2.)

Proving it:

  • What do you print each time damage lands, so you can count hits per second against your cooldown knob?
Do not reach for a manager. StatManager.cs is still an empty stub with no health in it and no method to change anything. Health lives on PlayerController, where you put it in 2.2, and that is what you call. The manager earns its place in 5.3, when a scene change finally gives you a reason.

Save and play. Walk into an enemy and hold still. You should take one hit, then one more every cooldown interval — and when your health reaches zero, your death rule from 2.2 should fire exactly as it did for the hazard you built then.

Bug Hunt: The Unfair Grapple

  1. Remove the cooldown check and stand inside the enemy for three seconds at 60 frames per second. How many hits did you take, and what happened to your death rule from 2.2?
  2. Seed the cooldown's "last hurt" field with 0 and walk into the enemy on the very first frame of the scene. How long are you immune — and what did you just invent?
  3. Use OnTriggerEnter2D but leave Is Trigger unticked on the enemy's collider. What fires? What does the Console show?
  4. Change the tag check to a tag that does not exist. What is the symptom, how long does it take you to find it, and what single tool would shorten that search?
  5. Set the damage knob equal to the player's full starting health. What is the entire encounter now — and why is a one-hit kill a design statement rather than a bug?
  6. Remove the enemy's Rigidbody2D but keep its collider, then walk into it. Do you take damage? Explain the result using the rule from 2.1 and the movement method you chose for the player in 2.2 — if your answer depends on your player's body type, say so.
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Attack Design

  1. Should the enemy knock you backwards on contact? Which component would have to be nudged — and your Player's Rigidbody2D is Dynamic, so a push does move it. What would you have to change about the body before that stopped being true, and what else would that change break? Test it before you answer.
  2. Design a damage tier: an enemy near a turret deals two, a lone enemy deals one. Where must that difference live so that each instance in the scene can differ, and what does the prefab value then mean?
  3. Make the enemy deal damage only while it is chasing, so a patrolling guard is harmless. What state information does that need, and where does it live in the file you have right now?
  4. Can you narrate a full encounter out loud using only your field names: spawn, patrol, cross the aggro radius, chase, contact, damage, flee, chase ends? If a sentence needs a word that is not a field or a comparison, which field are you missing?
  5. Commit and push: "4.4: contact damage + cooldown".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare the four rows in the hazard table and say which one you chose, and why a moving hazard differs from a stationary one
  • Explain, in frames, what goes wrong without a damage cooldown
  • Explain what the cooldown's starting value means, and what seeding it to 0 costs the player
  • Show how your enemy reaches the player's health, and which GetComponent call you used
  • Explain why the enemy is not destroyed on contact when the bullet was
  • Narrate a whole encounter as fields and comparisons
  • Break this feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this feature came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
